marker.name: pys02 sc014
marker.comment: meaning it was safe or safer for foreign investors to invest in the country. This was a big deal because this was

marker.name: pys02 sc015
marker.comment: the first time in its history it had gotten this rating.

marker.name: pys02 sc016
marker.comment: And then just earlier this year, it actually started taking advantage of it.

marker.name: pys02 sc017
marker.comment: They sold $350 million in bonds on Wall Street

marker.name: pys02 sc018
marker.comment: to fund different infrastructure projects they wanted to carry out.

marker.name: pys02 sc019
marker.comment: It was on the right path and it was being trusted by world investors.

marker.name: pys02 sc020
marker.comment: And the economy was growing. The first half of this year was the strongest growth it has ever had in country's history.

marker.name: pys02 sc021
marker.comment: So good news was all around, but among all

marker.name: pys02 sc022
marker.comment: this good news, there was one bad news that no one knew about.

marker.name: pys02 sc023
marker.comment: That news was that one of the biggest banks in the country was hiding a lot of its problems.

marker.name: pys03 sc001
marker.comment: So let me give you some background on this bank.

marker.name: pys03 sc002
marker.comment: The bank was born in 1950.

marker.name: pys03 sc003
marker.comment: I'm just kidding. I'm not gonna give you guys the background because it's really not that important relating to this story.

marker.name: pys03 sc004
marker.comment: So let's just go over the important parts of the story.

marker.name: pys03 sc005
marker.comment: The bank was started a long time ago, it was very profitable, but technically, for a very long time, it wasn't technically a bank.

marker.name: pys03 sc006
marker.comment: It was just a company that was giving money out. It was giving loans out, kinda charging high interest rate, so a bit of a loan sharking.

marker.name: pys03 sc007
marker.comment: But this was like decades ago, so maybe that was a common thing. I'm not really sure. But that's what the company was.

marker.name: pys03 sc008
marker.comment: It was called Credit Central.

marker.name: pys03 sc009
marker.comment: But since this was not a bank, it can give money out as loans, but it cannot take in deposits, because for that you need a license.

marker.name: pys03 sc010
marker.comment: And that's important. We'll talk about that in just a second.

marker.name: pys03 sc011
marker.comment: But as I said, this was an old company, it's been a part of this family for a very long time. But in 2015, the leadership changes.

marker.name: pys03 sc012
marker.comment: A new member of the family takes over the company,

marker.name: pys03 sc013
marker.comment: and his goals are very different than the people before him. He wanted to use the profits that this company was producing and

marker.name: pys03 sc014
marker.comment: try to create like a national conglomerate of different businesses.

marker.name: pys03 sc015
marker.comment: So he puts the bank in this new group that he starts, which is called the Vasquez group, and then he starts starting a bunch of businesses, starts buying a bunch of different things.

marker.name: pys03 sc016
marker.comment: The goal is to basically diversify the business away from this one thing that's making money.

marker.name: pys03 sc017
marker.comment: Take that money, invest in different industries, and hopefully become a major group,

marker.name: pys03 sc018
marker.comment: like we have in other countries, especially outside of the United States.

marker.name: pys03 sc019
marker.comment: A lot of Asian countries and even South American countries, even in the Middle East, it's a very common phenomenon

marker.name: pys03 sc020
marker.comment: where one big group controlled by one family or multiple families basically controls like every big business that's in that country.

marker.name: pys03 sc021
marker.comment: So he wanted to do something similar. / Now, the problem with this idea is usually whenever you try to

marker.name: pys03 sc022
marker.comment: start a new business, it loses money, sometimes for a very long time before it becomes profitable.

marker.name: pys03 sc023
marker.comment: But that's not a problem, at least right now,

marker.name: pys03 sc024
marker.comment: because he has this business that's making a lot of money. But hopefully you guys are seeing where the problem starts from.

marker.name: pys04 sc001
marker.comment: By 2020, around COVID times,

marker.name: pys04 sc002
marker.comment: he gets tired of not being a bank because he cannot take in deposits.

marker.name: pys04 sc003
marker.comment: And if you had deposits, you would just grow a lot faster.

marker.name: pys04 sc004
marker.comment: So in 2021, he merges this credit center thing that he has with a bank that already existed but was struggling.

marker.name: pys04 sc005
marker.comment: But this bank has the license to take in deposits. It was a real bank.

marker.name: pys04 sc006
marker.comment: So he merges these two companies

marker.name: pys04 sc007
marker.comment: and then he creates the bank that we are talking about. Ueno.

marker.name: pys04 sc008
marker.comment: This was gonna be like a modern bank that's kind of like a fintech, very focused on apps, websites, and online banking.

marker.name: pys04 sc009
marker.comment: This new bank starts doing really well, surprisingly well from the beginning.

marker.name: pys04 sc010
marker.comment: Maybe because it's one of the few banks in the country that's like online focused.

marker.name: pys04 sc011
marker.comment: And on top of that, it's running like crazy promos.

marker.name: pys04 sc012
marker.comment: One of the promos … if you're a new customer … open an account … anything you spend on the credit card, you get 50% back.

marker.name: pys04 sc013
marker.comment: So you could spend your money and you're basically getting a 50% discount.

marker.name: pys04 sc014
marker.comment: Now, of course, there were limits to this promo, meaning you couldn't go buy a private jet or a car or a house and get 50% off,

marker.name: pys04 sc015
marker.comment: but nonetheless, this was still a very, very lucrative promo for getting people in the door.

marker.name: pys04 sc016
marker.comment: And more importantly, this was really focused on like daily necessities like groceries, gas, the stuff people would buy every single day or every single week.

marker.name: pys04 sc017
marker.comment: And because of that, the bank started attracting a lot of people who were low income,

marker.name: pys04 sc018
marker.comment: but it made a huge difference to them

marker.name: pys04 sc019
marker.comment: when they got 50% off their monthly grocery bill or something like that, right?

marker.name: pys04 sc020
marker.comment: Now this was interesting because the bank was doing something very unique in the country.

marker.name: pys04 sc021
marker.comment: It was convincing a lot of people who never had a bank account to start opening their first ever bank accounts with this bank.

marker.name: pys04 sc022
marker.comment: Definitely a positive news but it creates a problem down the line.

marker.name: pys04 sc023
marker.comment: For now, the bank is on a very good trajectory and it's on such a good trajectory that

marker.name: pys04 sc024
marker.comment: few years after launching this new thing, this small bank ends up buying a bank that's four times bigger than it.

marker.name: pys04 sc025
marker.comment: Which was kind of a head scratcher when I first read the news

marker.name: pys04 sc026
marker.comment: because how the hell do you buy something that's four times bigger than you?

marker.name: pys05 sc001
marker.comment: Well this is where we need to talk about the secret weapon that this bank had and that has to do with its political capital.

marker.name: pys05 sc002
marker.comment: You see if we back up just a few years to like 2019, 2020,

marker.name: pys05 sc003
marker.comment: the original bank that we talked about, Credit Central, they got an investment from some outside investors. And one of those investors was

marker.name: pys05 sc004
marker.comment: then finance minister of the country Who goes on to become the president of the country in 2023.

marker.name: pys05 sc005
marker.comment: So again, the president says that he had never had a direct investment in this Weno Bank, or he was never directly involved.

marker.name: pys05 sc006
marker.comment: But between you and I, I think we can all imagine why this is such a beneficial thing for any company.

marker.name: pys05 sc007
marker.comment: Not just the bank. It's definitely a beneficial thing for any company when the president of the country, when the president of the country is one of your investors, right?

marker.name: pys05 sc008
marker.comment: So this was a very valuable political capital that they had, but it wasn't just that that they had.

marker.name: pys05 sc009
marker.comment: You see, in 2023, when President Penya won his election,

marker.name: pys05 sc010
marker.comment: the CEO of the bank was then picked to become the head of the central bank of the country. So he resigns his CEO post, and the next day he becomes part of the central bank that's supposed to be regulating this bank.

marker.name: pys05 sc011
marker.comment: Again, very, very valuable political capital.

marker.name: pys05 sc012
marker.comment: In any business, if the regulator is one of the guys who used to run your business.

marker.name: pys05 sc013
marker.comment: No matter what they say, that's a valuable thing. Well, that's exactly why they're able to, you know, do so many bigger things.

marker.name: pys05 sc014
marker.comment: They were able to buy a company that's four times bigger than them.

marker.name: pys05 sc015
marker.comment: Now, of course, the company they do buy is struggling a bit, but nonetheless,

marker.name: pys05 sc016
marker.comment: it is crazy that a bank that's four times smaller is buying something that's four times bigger.

marker.name: pys05 sc017
marker.comment: Now, this acquisition did not go according to plan. For multiple different reasons, but the biggest ones being that,

marker.name: pys05 sc018
marker.comment: first of all, UNO was an online focused bank, so it didn't really have expenses that a normal bank had.

marker.name: pys05 sc019
marker.comment: Well, it got those expenses when it bought this bigger bank, expenses like more people, branches, I'm sure other real estate.

marker.name: pys05 sc020
marker.comment: And on top of that, the bank they buy was struggling.

marker.name: pys05 sc021
marker.comment: And on top of that, the bank had already used a lot of their cash to survive before it sold to Wano.

marker.name: pys05 sc022
marker.comment: So this bank that they're absorbing is much bigger than them, and on top of that, it's in a much worse position than any bank should have been.

marker.name: pys06 sc001
marker.comment: Luckily for Ueno though, it had that political capital that we talked about,

marker.name: pys06 sc002
marker.comment: and that capital was about to turn into real cash.

marker.name: pys06 sc003
marker.comment: You see, after President Peña and his people took over the presidency,

marker.name: pys06 sc004
marker.comment: Ueno suddenly started getting a lot of deposits from government agencies, one of them being

marker.name: pys06 sc005
marker.comment: IPS, which is the National Security Institute for Paraguay.

marker.name: pys06 sc006
marker.comment: This is just pensions for citizens.

marker.name: pys06 sc007
marker.comment: Now, the pension fund has a lot of laws around it, basically to stop stuff like what we're about to see.

marker.name: pys06 sc008
marker.comment: But all those laws very quickly get changed to make it possible for the money to go into this singular bank.

marker.name: pys06 sc009
marker.comment: Now, one of the law was basically you don't want

marker.name: pys06 sc010
marker.comment: all the pension money sitting in one bank. So the rule said that you cannot have 10% of the whole fund with any single bank. You have to spread it out in case something happens to the bank, you don't want to lose everything overnight.

marker.name: pys06 sc011
marker.comment: Well, guess what? That law gets changed,

marker.name: pys06 sc012
marker.comment: and Ueno ends up getting roughly 30% of the entire pension money that the fund had.

marker.name: pys06 sc013
marker.comment: Now, on top of this, there was also

marker.name: pys06 sc014
marker.comment: a condition around the fund that basically said that you cannot really put your money with banks that are not like super, super, super safe.

marker.name: pys06 sc015
marker.comment: So you do want to put your money with banks that are really big and really, you know, stable.

marker.name: pys06 sc016
marker.comment: Unfortunately, Ueno was a new bank, it was growing very fast. That meant that it wasn't really super safe.

marker.name: pys06 sc017
marker.comment: But then again, this law was basically stepped aside to make sure the deposits keep on flowing into Ueno.

marker.name: pys06 sc018
marker.comment: Now, this was already raising eyebrows like two years ago, right when this started happening.

marker.name: pys06 sc019
marker.comment: So people were out there protesting,

marker.name: pys06 sc020
marker.comment: and people are out there saying that this looks sketchy

marker.name: pys06 sc021
marker.comment: because it seems the president was an investor in this bank, probably still is an investor,

marker.name: pys06 sc022
marker.comment: and now this bank that president says he's not involved in

marker.name: pys06 sc023
marker.comment: is getting all these deposits from government agencies.

marker.name: pys07 sc001
marker.comment: Now, with the benefit of hindsight, we actually have exact data

marker.name: pys07 sc002
marker.comment: …as to how long the president was investor for. And it wasn't until March 2025. … So roughly two years after becoming the president,

marker.name: pys07 sc002n
marker.comment: That president actually sells his stake.

marker.name: pys07 sc003
marker.comment: he was still a private investor in this bank that was getting a lot of money from the government.

marker.name: pys07 sc004
marker.comment: So definitely something you can easily say why this is a conflict of interest.

marker.name: pys07 sc005
marker.comment: But you see, this wasn't the only law or the requirement that this bank was breaking. In Paraguay,

marker.name: pys07 sc006
marker.comment: this is like a pretty strong law that the central bank has put down,

marker.name: pys07 sc007
marker.comment: basically saying that the ratio between a bank's equity and debt has to be 12% of above.

marker.name: pys07 sc008
marker.comment: In simple words … the cash bank has or any short term assets … has to be at least 12% of all the money that it has given out in loans.

marker.name: pys07 sc009
marker.comment: Now, all this time, until the very end, Ueno was saying

marker.name: pys07 sc010
marker.comment: that it was following all these ratios, right? It was above board.

marker.name: pys07 sc011
marker.comment: In fact, it was reporting that its ratio was 15%, and on top of that, the bad loans … were just 0.58%. So nearly half a percent.

marker.name: pys07 sc012
marker.comment: Now, this sounds really good. But if you start

marker.name: pys07 sc013
marker.comment: …looking closely, which no one actually did until recently, it's like suspiciously good.

marker.name: pys07 sc014
marker.comment: Any normal healthy bank in South America would have a bad loan ratio of 2 to 4%. So when Ueno is reporting just 0.5%,

marker.name: pys07 sc015
marker.comment: someone should have been asking, basically, wait, this just sounds too good to be true.

marker.name: pys07 sc016
marker.comment: And guess what? It was.

marker.name: pys08 sc001
marker.comment: And now this is where we come back to the beginning of the story.

marker.name: pys08 sc002
marker.comment: And remember how we talked about the family that owned this bank wants to start this conglomerate in the country, and because of that,

marker.name: pys08 sc003
marker.comment: they started multiple different businesses, and they were funding it all using the money they were getting from their profitable business.

marker.name: pys08 sc004
marker.comment: Well, guess what? All those businesses are still losing money, and on top of that,

marker.name: pys08 sc005
marker.comment: all those other businesses have taken out big loans from this bank that we're talking about, Ueno.

marker.name: pys08 sc006
marker.comment: So there were media companies, tech companies, software companies, anything you can imagine.

marker.name: pys08 sc007
marker.comment: All these businesses were just getting loans from the bank and trying to basically become a big company in their field.

marker.name: pys08 sc008
marker.comment: Now. Technically speaking, and according to Paraguay's law, this is not illegal.

marker.name: pys08 sc009
marker.comment: A bank can technically give money to companies that it's related to, meaning it has the same owner with, but it can only do so with the 2%

marker.name: pys08 sc010
marker.comment: …of the deposits this has. So as long as the loans you're giving out to yourself, or as some people call it self-dealing, … below 20%, it's legal. But if it goes above that, that's illegal.

marker.name: pys08 sc011
marker.comment: Now this law is about to become a big problem because all these other businesses are

marker.name: pys08 sc012
marker.comment: struggling very badly and they need money to survive. And bank actually needs these businesses to survive if it wants to survive itself.

marker.name: pys08 sc013
marker.comment: This is where I want to share the famous quote about banking that I'm sure you've heard.

marker.name: pys08 sc014
marker.comment: Where if you owe a million dollars to a bank, that's your problem. But if you owe a billion dollars to a bank, that's banks' problem. That's the exact case.

marker.name: pys08 sc015
marker.comment: Since these companies owed so much money to the bank, bank literally could not afford to have these companies go out.

marker.name: pys08 sc016
marker.comment: But legally speaking, it cannot also give more money to these companies because. It's not allowed to.

marker.name: pys08 sc017
marker.comment: So what it does is basically start doing stuff illegally.

marker.name: pys08 sc018
marker.comment: The family that owns the whole thing, they start creating shell companies, fake companies with just random people who are owners.

marker.name: pys08 sc019
marker.comment: When I say random people, I mean low-level employees at these companies who are owners.

marker.name: pys08 sc020
marker.comment: And then out of nowhere, it's like a company is created today, the very next day this company has no money, no business, … it gets tens of millions of dollars in loans.

marker.name: pys08 sc021
marker.comment: And then after a lot of [re]routing of that money, that money ends up at the company that needs the money to pay payroll to carry out businesses.

marker.name: pys08 sc022
marker.comment: So technically speaking, they're doing all this shell company business

marker.name: pys08 sc023
marker.comment: just to loan the money to a company that they're not supposed to loan the money to.

marker.name: pys09 sc001
marker.comment: In reality, this problem should not have continued for very long because whenever you loan someone

marker.name: pys09 sc002
marker.comment: this kind of fake money … run this money through this fake business,

marker.name: pys09 sc003
marker.comment: if they don't make loan payments in less, say 60 days, legally speaking,

marker.name: pys09 sc004
marker.comment: you're supposed to write down that loan, basically count it as a loss. You're not getting money, it's bad debt.

marker.name: pys09 sc005
marker.comment: You have to tell the accountant, you have to tell the regulators, you have to tell your investors,

marker.name: pys09 sc006
marker.comment: saying, Hey, bad mistake on our part.

marker.name: pys09 sc007
marker.comment: This was a bad loan. We're gonna take this down as a loss. But this is where you can get creative.

marker.name: pys09 sc008
marker.comment: And this is where I want to share the quote I've shared before.

marker.name: pys09 sc009
marker.comment: My accounting teacher, first thing she said when I walked into the class was basically, you guys know what happens to creative accountants?

marker.name: pys09 sc010
marker.comment: they go to jail.

marker.name: pys09 sc011
marker.comment: I don't know if that happens in the United States, but it does happen in Paraguay,

marker.name: pys09 sc012
marker.comment: because people are about to get creative and they're gonna end up in jail, I feel like.

marker.name: pys09 sc013
marker.comment: So the new creative way they came up with … creating fake companies, moving money to the company, then giving it to the company that needs it over and over again.

marker.name: pys09 sc014
marker.comment: So whenever a loan was supposed to make payments, the company did not have any money to make the payment with.

marker.name: pys09 sc015
marker.comment: So instead of … saying this is bad loan, we're gonna write it down, they just issued new loans to that same company, and then that company used that money to pay back the bank, and then bank basically said, Hey, old loan, it's good.

marker.name: pys09 sc016
marker.comment: But now we have this new loan that's — we'll see if it's good or not.

marker.name: pys09 sc017
marker.comment: So they just kept delaying the problem.

marker.name: pys09 sc018
marker.comment: until everything got too big to fail.

marker.name: pys09 sc019
marker.comment: By the end of it all, they had given out more than three hundred million dollars using this scheme to companies that they own themselves.

marker.name: pys09 sc020
marker.comment: The bank was basically lending money to a company so they could pay the bank back so they could borrow more money. This actually has a name: Merry go around.

marker.name: pys10 sc001
marker.comment: Now luckily the central bank did catch on what was going on and they stepped in

marker.name: pys10 sc002
marker.comment: because they were able to trace that all that money … ended up where it's not supposed to, legally speaking,

marker.name: pys10 sc003
marker.comment: because while they were loaning out money, they were reporting something entirely different to the central bank.

marker.name: pys10 sc004
marker.comment: But when you look into it you realize that hey this bank is actually lying.

marker.name: pys10 sc005
marker.comment: So the central bank tell this bank … you need to do something about these loans that you have given out.

marker.name: pys10 sc006
marker.comment: You have two options. First you have to declare that these loans are bad loans, meaning you have to write it down as a loss on your income sheet.

marker.name: pys10 sc007
marker.comment: That would mean that the bank would basically stop being a bank because it has lost too much money.

marker.name: pys10 sc008
marker.comment: So it would have to … it's breaking too many laws, too many requirements, the capital ratio requirement we talked about,

marker.name: pys10 sc009
marker.comment: and it would just basically have to give itself over to the government to do what they're doing right now.

marker.name: pys10 sc010
marker.comment: Or the central bank gave the bank a second option.

marker.name: pys10 sc011
marker.comment: Second option was basically you can survive if you can find a company or a bank that's willing to buy out these loans that you have.

marker.name: pys10 sc012
marker.comment: Now, in reality, the loan was a piece of [BLEEP]. No one actually wants to buy it because it's not an asset. It's just fake companies getting a lot of money.

marker.name: pys10 sc013
marker.comment: But somehow, some way, Ueno is able to find a buyer.

marker.name: pys10 sc014
marker.comment: But you see, this buyer is also of very suspicious origins.

marker.name: pys10 sc015
marker.comment: So the company that ends up buying these loans is a company that's owned by the same group that own the bank.

marker.name: pys10 sc016
marker.comment: And as if this wasn't bad enough, just a few days ago, before this company buys the loans, it had no money.

marker.name: pys10 sc017
marker.comment: This new company had no money. It had like 100,000, less than 100,000 in cash.

marker.name: pys10 sc018
marker.comment: And then out of nowhere, Ueno. Loans money to bunch of shell companies, and that money somehow ends up in this new company.

marker.name: pys10 sc019
marker.comment: So around 79 million dollars of money this new company uses to buy the loans from this Ueno bank that the central bank was telling it to sell.

marker.name: pys10 sc020
marker.comment: So in simple terms, Ueno just ended up using its own money to buy its own piece of [BLEEP]

marker.name: pys10 sc021
marker.comment: and tell the central bank, hey, look, this is valuable, someone's paying us 80 million dollars for it.

marker.name: pys10 sc022
marker.comment: People on the ground who were investigating all this, or the regulators who were looking over all this, they very quickly realized what was going on.

marker.name: pys10 sc023
marker.comment: You know, they were using their own money to buy their own bad loans.

marker.name: pys10 sc024
marker.comment: So they wrote up a report and sent the report to the head of the central bank.

marker.name: pys10 sc025
marker.comment: But guess what we talked about earlier?

marker.name: pys10 sc026
marker.comment: The head of the central bank was literally the CEO of this bank that we are talking about.

marker.name: pys10 sc027
marker.comment: He was the CEO of Ueno on August 14th, two years ago. On August 15th, he becomes the head of the central bank.

marker.name: pys10 sc028
marker.comment: So there is no gap here.

marker.name: pys10 sc029
marker.comment: So he basically buries the report.

marker.name: pys10 sc030
marker.comment: Now we don't know this for sure, so I have to say allegedly, but. Hopefully you and I understand what's going on here.

marker.name: pys10 sc031
marker.comment: Investigations are still going on, so I don't want to say anything that's breaking any laws,

marker.name: pys10 sc032
marker.comment: but I think people understand what's going on here.

marker.name: pys11 sc001
marker.comment: So now I'm sure some of you guys are maybe asking, how does this whole thing fall apart if the guy's trying to bury it all?

marker.name: pys11 sc002
marker.comment: Well, two months after this report was buried by the head of the bank.

marker.name: pys11 sc003
marker.comment: The guy who wrote this report actually ends up getting moved out of the department.

marker.name: pys11 sc004
marker.comment: But two months after this whole thing happens,

marker.name: pys11 sc005
marker.comment: somehow, some way, that report makes its way to a news organization or a newspaper in Paraguay.

marker.name: pys11 sc006
marker.comment: One of the oldest and one of the biggest. It's called ABC Color.

marker.name: pys11 sc007
marker.comment: And all that story I just told you guys is because

marker.name: pys11 sc008
marker.comment: once this organization got this report, they published it

marker.name: pys11 sc009
marker.comment: and they just kept on investigation to find everything else that happened around it.

marker.name: pys11 sc010
marker.comment: So all the details we know is because of the media. We don't know this because the government is telling us.

marker.name: pys11 sc011
marker.comment: I'm sure the government is gonna do its investigation on its own

marker.name: pys11 sc012
marker.comment: and publish it later down the line, but remember.

marker.name: pys11 sc013
marker.comment: This whole thing just happened last week. So the fact that we know all this is all thanks to the media that the country has.

marker.name: pys11 sc014
marker.comment: Now, when this report is made public and when subsequent investigations are made public,

marker.name: pys11 sc015
marker.comment: it just breaks the political back of the country.

marker.name: pys11 sc016
marker.comment: The political pressure is coming down on everyone involved. The central bank, the president, and anyone else who's not speaking up … on the side of the president.

marker.name: pys11 sc017
marker.comment: In fact, senators from his own party

marker.name: pys11 sc018
marker.comment: actually formally request an investigation into everything that's going on, and they ask the central bank to basically figure out,

marker.name: pys11 sc019
marker.comment: hey, is this bank actually good?

marker.name: pys11 sc020
marker.comment: Because this is one of the biggest banks in the country.

marker.name: pys12 sc001
marker.comment: Now, while all this investigation is going on,

marker.name: pys12 sc002
marker.comment: we also need to talk about Paraguay's place in international finance.

marker.name: pys12 sc003
marker.comment: You see, it's still a developing country,

marker.name: pys12 sc004
marker.comment: meaning foreign investors don't really trust the government and institutions inside of this country as much as they would trust, let's say institutions inside of the United States or European countries.

marker.name: pys12 sc005
marker.comment: And because of that, what foreign investors really depend on is the IMF assessment.

marker.name: pys12 sc006
marker.comment: If IMF is saying that hey this is a good country,

marker.name: pys12 sc007
marker.comment: that's a huge benefit to any country that gets that sign of approval

marker.name: pys12 sc008
marker.comment: because it lowers their borrowing rate, and that means they can just fund future expansion. They can take on loans to fund infrastructure and stuff like that.

marker.name: pys12 sc009
marker.comment: So whatever IMF says is very important, and to give its assessment,

marker.name: pys12 sc010
marker.comment: every year IMF sends its people to these countries once a year to just go make sure everything is good.

marker.name: pys12 sc011
marker.comment: You know, government is not lying, there's not too much corruption … institutions are working properly, courts are working, they just go through their checklist.

marker.name: pys12 sc012
marker.comment: Well, for Paraguay, that assessment was taking place

marker.name: pys12 sc013
marker.comment: literally last week when this news became breaking news.

marker.name: pys12 sc014
marker.comment: So IMF assessment people, assessors were in the country

marker.name: pys12 sc015
marker.comment: while the central bank was being asked by the Senate of the country to do something about all these reports that are coming out.

marker.name: pys12 sc016
marker.comment: So there was a lot of political pressure on the central bank to not mess it up, you know, not bury it.

marker.name: pys12 sc017
marker.comment: Because if they bury it, it kind of looks like corruption. And then it becomes a much bigger problem than it already is.

marker.name: pys12 sc018
marker.comment: Because right now, if you take care of this problem, it looks like one bad bank. But if you try to bury it, everyone's questioning is this one bad bank? Or every bank in the country is like that. Or if the whole government is like that.

marker.name: pys12 sc019
marker.comment: So that's why the central bank could not actually bury this or figure out some way to keep it quiet.

marker.name: pys12 sc020
marker.comment: They had to make it seem like this was just a one bank problem.

marker.name: pys12 sc021
marker.comment: On top of that, this is a common occurrence,

marker.name: pys12 sc022
marker.comment: meaning banking crises like these ones have happened before in Paraguay.

marker.name: pys12 sc023
marker.comment: And because of that, they have a very unique law that other countries don't really have

marker.name: pys12 sc024
marker.comment: when in reality in my opinion I think they should have. More countries should take over this law.

marker.name: pys12 sc025
marker.comment: This law basically says that hey if you're on the board of the central bank and if you know something under the table … you're going to be criminally held liable whenever the thing blows apart.

marker.name: pys12 sc026
marker.comment: and you don't do anything about it,

marker.name: pys12 sc028
marker.comment: Meaning all the people on the board have now a personal incentive or I guess disincentive

marker.name: pys12 sc029
marker.comment: to make sure that they do what they're supposed to do instead of trying to bury this

marker.name: pys12 sc030
marker.comment: because if this thing becomes bigger than what it is right now

marker.name: pys12 sc031
marker.comment: everyone could face criminal charges in the future.

marker.name: pys13 sc001
marker.comment: So if you combine all of this, the board basically does the right thing

marker.name: pys13 sc002
marker.comment: despite the fact that the head of the board is the former CEO of the Ueno bank.

marker.name: pys13 sc003
marker.comment: Board basically votes unanimously saying that this is a bad bank.

marker.name: pys13 sc004
marker.comment: The government is gonna take it over and they're gonna figure out how they can make everyone whole

marker.name: pys13 sc005
marker.comment: everyone who deposited with the bank, they're gonna figure out what's the best way to take care of this bankruptcy.

marker.name: pys13 sc006
marker.comment: This could mean many sorts of thing, right? We don't exactly know what's gonna happen in the future.

marker.name: pys13 sc007
marker.comment: But one thing was clear,

marker.name: pys13 sc008
marker.comment: the bank is done.

marker.name: pys13 sc009
marker.comment: People started logging into their accounts, checking their apps and it would just not work. You couldn't see your balance,

marker.name: pys13 sc010
marker.comment: you couldn't draw money, you couldn't do anything,

marker.name: pys13 sc011
marker.comment: and this created a big problem in the country because as I said before

marker.name: pys13 sc012
marker.comment: a lot of people had their money in this bank and on top of that a lot of low income people had their money in the bank

marker.name: pys13 sc013
marker.comment: meaning even if they know they're gonna get their money back because of the national insurance thing … the FDIC of Paraguay

marker.name: pys13 sc014
marker.comment: they don't have money in their hands to just live their life, you know

marker.name: pys13 sc015
marker.comment: to buy groceries, to buy gas, to buy whatever normal things people buy so

marker.name: pys13 sc016
marker.comment: if they can't access their money in the bank they can wait for weeks or months whatever it's gonna take for the government to figure all this out

marker.name: pys13 sc017
marker.comment: and that's why we are seeing protest all over the place.

marker.name: pys13 sc018
marker.comment: Now regulators have come up with different solutions as to how to deal with this problem.

marker.name: pys13 sc019
marker.comment: One of them is they're gonna start giving people just like $1500 or something so they can continue their monthly expenses.

marker.name: pys13 sc020
marker.comment: But as I said before, a lot of the people that this bank had they don't have any of their accounts

marker.name: pys13 sc021
marker.comment: I'm sure they'll figure it out

marker.name: pys13 sc022
marker.comment: but but it creates chaos, uncertainty and people are scared.

marker.name: pys13 sc023
marker.comment: Now arrests are being made.

marker.name: pys13 sc024
marker.comment: the president tried resigning because if he is able to resign he gets immunity for life

marker.name: pys13 sc025
marker.comment: meaning nothing's gonna happen to him,

marker.name: pys13 sc026
marker.comment: but the Senate rejects his resignation and then impeaches him.

marker.name: pys13 sc027
marker.comment: So now he does not have that immunity

marker.name: pys13 sc028
marker.comment: and he's under house arrest while the investigation is ongoing.

marker.name: pys13 sc029
marker.comment: The head of the board, former CEO of Ueno bank, is under arrest.

marker.name: pys13 sc030
marker.comment: The family member, the guy who owned the whole thing, he's under arrest now.

marker.name: pys13 sc031
marker.comment: And twenty or so people are also under arrest who are involved in different different companies and banks who are making these decisions.

marker.name: pys13 sc032
marker.comment: So investigation is ongoing. I'm sure we'll find out more,

marker.name: pys13 sc033
marker.comment: but definitely a very interesting story that came out.

marker.name: pys13 sc034
marker.comment: Now, on top of this, there's another part of the story that's going viral, and that is

marker.name: pys13 sc035
marker.comment: the daughter of the president was actually here in the United States. She's 20 years old, so very young.

marker.name: pys13 sc036
marker.comment: People do stupid [BLEEP] when they're young a lot. I've done a lot. But

marker.name: pys13 sc037
marker.comment: on her Instagram, she posted a picture saying tax the poor.

marker.name: pys13 sc038
marker.comment: And that's a picture that Paraguayan people are not happy about,

marker.name: pys13 sc039
marker.comment: and people at Columbia, so the university here in the United States are also not happy about.

marker.name: pys13 sc040
marker.comment: So she's going viral on social media too, which is just adding more fire to the story that people are already mad about.
